newsitem.title: AUSTRALIA: FEATURE - Australian pearl industry shines.
newsitem.headline: FEATURE - Australian pearl industry shines.

text.p: Australia's once secretive pearling industry has overcome more than a century of suspicion and dirty tricks to forge a new alliance to take on the rest of the world.

Leading pearl producers have banded together to form the South Sea Pearl Consortium, a non-profit group aimed at expanding the country's A$200 million-a-year pearl industry and snatching a bigger market share for Australian South Sea pearl exports.
Consortium chairman Nicholas Paspaley said producers had decided the long-term prosperity of the industry was more important than short-term gains for individual companies.
"We have to look after the market," Paspaley told Reuters in the Northern Territory capital, Darwin, headquarters of his diversified business empire.
"And that sometimes means doing what's good for the long term and making sacrifices."
Paspaley heads Australia's biggest pearl producer, Paspaley Pearling Co, valued at about A$130 million and with a 60 percent share of the country's production.
Since commercial pearling began off Australia's remote and rugged northern coast last century, it has been a rough and tumble industry.

For years, pearlers jealously guarded their best oyster grounds, boat designs and production techniques. Their rivals poached production secrets and copied boat designs; sometimes, oysters themselves would disappear overnight.
But the industry has developed rapidly over the past two decades, transformed by capital injections, international partnerships, tight government monitoring and advances in technology and farming.
Production is booming.

Although accounting for barely one percent of total world pearl tonnage, the value of Australian production surged 60 percent to A$196 million in 1994/95, the last year for which official figures are available, from A$122 million in 1993/94.
Industry sources say this growth is being maintained.
The Darwin-based South Sea Pearl Consortium was formed last year to promote and market Australian South Sea pearls.
Australia is the world's leading producer of the large South Sea pearls.

The group was founded by Paspaley, Australian company Broome Pearls Pty Ltd, Japan's Nippo Pearl Co and Hamaguchi Pearling Co, U.S. company Assael International Inc and Cogent Trading Co Ltd of Hong Kong.

The consortium says the unpolluted waters and huge tidal flows off the remote northern coast, home to most of the country's pearl farms, produce a healthier oyster, which means a larger and superior pearl.
"Our environment is superior, our farm sites are very good," said John Kelly, managing director the country's second-largest producer, Broome Pearls.
The consortium is initially targeting the key markets of Hong Kong, Japan and the United States.
A single top quality Australian South Sea pearl can fetch up to US$70,000 and an 18-pearl necklace up to US$2.25 million.

But the consortium is also developing a marketing strategy and niche-targeted jewellery priced about US$400-$450 aimed at young professional women, said the group's international manager, Chryss Carr.
"We want to market the pearl in a contemporary fashion and bring it to the forefront of fashion again," she said.

It has enlisted the help of rising Australian designer Collette Dinnigan to target this new market. Dinnigan designed a range of pearl jewellery to go with her spring/summer 1997 collection, which debuted on the Paris catwalk in October.
